question: A woman on long-term treatment for rheumatoid arthritis was hospitalised in the past for a gastric ulcer. Considering that history, which of the following drugs would be the most suitable for controlling her joint disease?
explanation: Celecoxib spares COX-1, the isoform that maintains the protective gastric mucus and bicarbonate layer, so it delivers anti-inflammatory benefit with markedly fewer ulcers and bleeds. That makes it the preferred NSAID when peptic ulcer disease is in the history.

explanations.A: Celecoxib spares COX-1, the isoform that maintains the protective gastric mucus and bicarbonate layer, so it delivers anti-inflammatory benefit with markedly fewer ulcers and bleeds. That makes it the preferred NSAID when peptic ulcer disease is in the history.
explanations.B: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist used to reverse respiratory depression. It has neither analgesic nor anti-inflammatory activity and no place in arthritis.
explanations.C: Paracetamol is gastric-friendly but barely anti-inflammatory, so it cannot control the synovitis that drives joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis.
explanations.D: Ibuprofen blocks COX-1 as well as COX-2 and would clearly raise the chance of ulcer recurrence and gastrointestinal haemorrhage in a patient already sensitised.

question: Among the drugs used in the standard first-line regimen for tuberculosis, which one is considered to have the greatest bactericidal power against the tubercle bacillus?
explanation: Rifampicin blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and kills bacilli wherever they sit, whether multiplying briskly in cavities, lying semi-dormant in caseous foci or hiding inside macrophages. This breadth of killing, plus its powerful sterilising effect that permits short-course therapy, is why it is ranked the most bactericidal of the first-line drugs.

explanations.A: Rifampicin blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and kills bacilli wherever they sit, whether multiplying briskly in cavities, lying semi-dormant in caseous foci or hiding inside macrophages. This breadth of killing, plus its powerful sterilising effect that permits short-course therapy, is why it is ranked the most bactericidal of the first-line drugs.
explanations.B: Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase and is essentially bacteriostatic at usual doses. It is added mainly to protect the companion drugs against emerging resistance.
explanations.C: Isoniazid is strongly cidal against rapidly dividing extracellular bacilli and in fact shows the highest early bactericidal activity in the first two days of treatment, but its reach into slow-growing and intracellular populations is narrower than that of rifampicin.
explanations.D: Pyrazinamide comes into its own only in the acidic environment inside macrophages and inflamed lesions, killing the persisters that shorten therapy. Outside that niche it is largely inactive, so it is not the most bactericidal drug overall.

question: A nurse is reviewing the safe ways of giving calcium gluconate. Which one of the following methods of administration must be avoided for this drug?
explanation: A rapid bolus floods the myocardium with calcium and provokes bradycardia, flushing, hypotension and, at worst, arrest in systole. The risk is greatest in a digitalised patient, so calcium is never pushed fast, and the ECG is watched while it runs.

explanations.A: A rapid bolus floods the myocardium with calcium and provokes bradycardia, flushing, hypotension and, at worst, arrest in systole. The risk is greatest in a digitalised patient, so calcium is never pushed fast, and the ECG is watched while it runs.
explanations.B: A slow, diluted intravenous push spread over roughly 5 to 10 minutes is the accepted way to stabilise the myocardium in hyperkalaemia or to abort tetany.
explanations.C: For symptomatic hypocalcaemia the drug is diluted in dextrose or saline and infused over 30 to 60 minutes, which keeps the plasma level rising gently.
explanations.D: Oral calcium salts are entirely appropriate for maintenance and for chronic hypocalcaemia once the emergency has passed.

question: Analgesia has to be planned for a patient who has a documented history of peptic ulcer disease. Which approach to pain relief carries the least risk for this patient?
explanation: Withholding NSAIDs altogether is the safest plan. Paracetamol is the preferred first-line agent, with an opioid added for severe pain; if an anti-inflammatory is truly unavoidable, a COX-2 selective agent under proton pump inhibitor cover is used with informed caution.

explanations.A: Non-selective NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, stripping the mucosa of the prostaglandins that maintain bicarbonate secretion, mucus and mucosal blood flow. In a patient who has already ulcerated, this invites recurrence, bleeding and perforation.
explanations.B: Withholding NSAIDs altogether is the safest plan. Paracetamol is the preferred first-line agent, with an opioid added for severe pain; if an anti-inflammatory is truly unavoidable, a COX-2 selective agent under proton pump inhibitor cover is used with informed caution.
explanations.C: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 for the life of the platelet, so it damages the mucosa and impairs haemostasis at the same time. It is the most ulcerogenic option listed.
explanations.D: A proton pump inhibitor substantially reduces, but does not abolish, NSAID-related mucosal injury, and it gives less protection in the distal small bowel and colon. Since the question asks for the safest option, avoidance still outranks NSAID plus PPI.

question: Which adverse effect do patients on nitroglycerin report most frequently?
explanation: Dilatation of meningeal vessels produces a throbbing, usually frontal headache, and it is the commonest complaint with every nitrate preparation. It tends to settle over days as tolerance to this effect develops, and paracetamol relieves it; patients are counselled not to abandon therapy because of it.

explanations.A: Nitrates lower blood pressure by venodilatation, and the baroreceptor response to this is reflex tachycardia. Bradycardia is not a typical nitrate effect and, when it appears with inferior wall infarction, it is a reason to withhold the drug.
explanations.B: Dilatation of meningeal vessels produces a throbbing, usually frontal headache, and it is the commonest complaint with every nitrate preparation. It tends to settle over days as tolerance to this effect develops, and paracetamol relieves it; patients are counselled not to abandon therapy because of it.
explanations.C: Nausea may accompany the hypotension or the headache but is distinctly less frequent than the headache itself.
explanations.D: Palpitations do occur through reflex sympathetic activation, particularly after a sublingual dose, but they are reported far less often than headache.

question: Of the first-line anti-tubercular agents listed below, which is bactericidal rather than merely bacteriostatic against Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
explanation: Both isoniazid and pyrazinamide are bactericidal, each acting on a different bacillary population, so the combined option is the complete answer.

explanations.A: Ethambutol is tuberculostatic and is included largely to hold back emergence of resistance, not for rapid killing.
explanations.B: Isoniazid is genuinely bactericidal against rapidly multiplying extracellular bacilli, but it is not the only bactericidal drug offered here.
explanations.C: Pyrazinamide kills semi-dormant bacilli in the acidic intracellular and caseous environment, which is why it allows therapy to be shortened to six months - again correct but incomplete on its own.
explanations.D: Both isoniazid and pyrazinamide are bactericidal, each acting on a different bacillary population, so the combined option is the complete answer.
